lessons.title: Strategic management of the farm business
lessons.html:
Strategic management

At N6 level the manager is expected to think and act strategically: to position the farm business for long-term success in a changing environment. Strategic management is a continuous process of analysis, choice, implementation and evaluation.

Environmental analysis

A PESTEL scan structures the external analysis:

  • Political – land reform policy, trade agreements, municipal service delivery.
  • Economic – interest and exchange rates, input costs, consumer spending.
  • Social – consumer preferences, rural labour availability, community relations.
  • Technological – precision agriculture, new cultivars, renewable energy.
  • Environmental – climate variability, water availability, biodiversity obligations.
  • Legal – labour, water, food safety and conservation law.

Industry analysis looks at the bargaining power of buyers (retailers, processors, exporters) and suppliers, competitors, substitutes and barriers to entry. Internal analysis identifies resources and capabilities that give an advantage, such as water rights, a strong brand, a skilled workforce or low-cost production.

Strategic options

StrategyFarm example
Cost leadershipLarge-scale grain production with efficient mechanisation
DifferentiationCertified organic or grass-fed beef sold at a premium
Vertical integrationAdding a packhouse, abattoir or own retail outlet
DiversificationAdding agri-tourism, a new crop or contracting services
CollaborationJoint ventures, study groups, shared marketing or equipment

Evaluating options

Test each option for suitability (does it fit the analysis and goals?), feasibility (are resources, skills and finance available?) and acceptability (returns, risk and stakeholder support). Use discounted cash flow analysis for major investments.

Implementation

Translate strategy into objectives, budgets, projects and responsibilities. A balanced scorecard can link financial, customer, internal process and learning-and-growth measures to strategy, so daily activity supports long-term direction.

lessons.title: Leadership, change and enterprise risk management
lessons.html:
Leadership

Leadership is the ability to influence people to achieve goals willingly. Farm managers lead diverse teams across cultures, languages and generations.

  • Situational leadership – adapt style to the follower's competence and commitment: directing for new workers, coaching and supporting as skills develop, delegating to experienced and committed staff.
  • Transformational leadership – inspire through a shared vision, personal example and developing people.
  • Ethical leadership – fairness, honesty and consistency build trust, which is essential in close-knit farm communities.

Motivation

Pay and conditions must be fair, but recognition, responsibility, skills development, career paths and good communication drive sustained performance. Incentive schemes should reward outcomes the business values, including quality and safety, not just volume.

Managing change

Introducing new technology, restructuring or changing enterprises meets resistance when people fear loss of income, status or security. Effective change management:

  1. Explains clearly why change is needed.
  2. Involves those affected early and listens to concerns.
  3. Provides training and resources.
  4. Pilots changes and shows early results.
  5. Follows the legal consultation requirements where jobs are affected.
  6. Reinforces new practices through systems and recognition.

Enterprise risk management

Risk management identifies, assesses, treats and monitors risks across the business.

RiskExample treatment
Production (drought, hail, disease)Insurance, irrigation, biosecurity, drought-tolerant cultivars, fodder reserves
Market (price falls, buyer failure)Forward contracts, several buyers, credit checks
Financial (rates, debt)Conservative gearing, cash reserves, stress tests
Human (injury, key staff loss)OHS systems, succession and cross-training
Legal and reputationalCompliance systems, audits, community engagement
Security (stock theft, crime)Branding and marking of livestock, patrols, community policing forums

A risk register scores each risk by likelihood and impact, names an owner and tracks treatments. Continuity plans cover events such as fire, floods, prolonged power outages and disease outbreaks requiring movement controls under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Succession

Many family farms fail at handover. Plan ownership, management and asset transfer early, with legal and tax advice.

Key points

  • Strategic management cycles through analysis, choice, implementation and evaluation.
  • Use PESTEL, industry and internal analysis to choose strategy.
  • Test options for suitability, feasibility and acceptability.
  • Adapt leadership style and manage change by involving people early.
  • Use a risk register and continuity and succession plans.
